common_name: Striped Agave (Narrow-Leaf Wild Striped Century Plant)

planting.note: Set out rooted offsets in spring once soil has warmed, in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; this naturally occurring striped variety stays noticeably narrower and more upright than the broad-leaved straight species.

directions: Agave americana var. striata is the wild-occurring striped form of the common century plant, distinguished from the plain species by narrower, more upright, gray-green leaves marked with fine ivory-white longitudinal striping along their length rather than only a marginal band. It is the naturally variegated source stock behind several of the better-known marginal and central-striped cultivars sold in the trade, though it breeds less uniformly than named clonal selections and plants grown from seed or offsets show some variability in stripe width. Grow it in the same lean, sharply drained, full-sun conditions as the species, where it is just as drought-tolerant and nearly as cold-hardy, and expect the same slow-growing, monocarpic life cycle that ends in a single tall flowering stalk after many years, with offsets persisting afterward to continue the clump.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Albifructus is a white-fruited sport of purple beautyberry and benefits from the same hard late-winter pruning to maximize berry set.

directions: Albifructus is a white-berried sport of purple beautyberry, carrying the same arching stems and whorled clusters as the typical violet-purple form but ripening to clean, porcelain-white drupes that stand out strikingly against the still-green autumn foliage and show especially well against a dark evergreen backdrop. Because it is a color sport rather than a seed strain, plants grown from seed can revert toward purple fruit, so propagation by cuttings is preferred to preserve the white color reliably. Cut stems back hard to 6-12 inches in late winter each year, as with the species, since the heaviest fruit set forms on vigorous current-season wood. The pale berries persist into early winter and are taken by birds somewhat later than the more conspicuous purple fruit, extending the shrub's season of interest.

planting.note: Divide rooted suckers or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained to dry soil in partial to full shade; Foliis Variegatis is a yellow-margined sport of native coralberry grown chiefly to brighten dark shade rather than for its modest flowers or fruit.

directions: Foliis Variegatis carries the same wiry, arching stems and suckering, colony-forming habit as plain coralberry, but each small oval leaf is irregularly edged in soft yellow, giving the planting a visibly lighter, variegated texture that reads well from a distance in the deep, dry shade where this species is normally grown as a workhorse groundcover. The yellow margin is most pronounced on new growth in spring and fades somewhat by late summer, though it remains a useful foliage accent even without reliable fruiting color. Like the straight species, it tolerates clay, alkaline soil, and root competition from mature trees better than almost any other deciduous shrub, spreading slowly by suckers to knit together a dry, shaded slope or understory planting. Because variegated growth is less vigorous than plain green coralberry, remove any reverted all-green suckers to keep the patterning dominant in the planting.

planting.note: Divide rooted suckers or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; Laciniata is a finely cut-leaved sumac selection that must be propagated vegetatively, since seedlings revert to the plain-leaved species.

directions: Laciniata is a long-cultivated cutleaf selection of staghorn sumac, its compound leaflets so deeply and finely incised that the whole frond takes on a soft, lacy, fern-like texture quite unlike the coarser, more tropical-looking foliage of the plain species. It carries the same velvety, antler-like branch tips, the same brilliant orange-to-scarlet fall color, and the same persistent, fuzzy crimson fruit cones valued by birds through winter, but the refined, dissected leaf texture gives it a markedly more delicate garden presence despite reaching the same eventual size. Because this trait does not come true from seed, propagate only from root cuttings or division of an existing clone to maintain the cutleaf character. Like the species it spreads by root suckers and is best sited where that colonizing habit can be tolerated or contained by mowing the perimeter.
